It is possible that the numbers of pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, and car drivers who travel within the streets where street lighting was reduced declined at the same time as the lighting was reduced, resulting in fewer collisions in those streets. If so, any increase in hazards to road users due to lower lighting conditions may have been obscured by a reduction in numbers of people exposed to road injury risk at night (Steinbach, 2015). However, qualitative and survey evidence (Perkins, 2015; Green, 2015) suggests that changes to mobility overall and mode choice in areas affected were likely to be minimal. One potential reason is that the impact may not be as direct as how crime and crash statistics or perceived security and safety impact travel mode and peoples’ desire to walk (recreational or utilitarian). But given the correlation between street lighting and safety and security, street 28 lighting may still play an important role in mobility and travel mode choice, as also evidenced by street lighting and physical activity review in the previous section. 2.3 Summary Based on the literature reviews of currently available research in the targeted areas, the following conclusions can be made: • Fatal and serious traffic injuries are higher at night than in daylight. A similar trend is observed for pedestrian fatalities. Without street lighting, pedestrian fatality probability per crash is almost 3 times higher in the dark. Researchers hypothesize that one of the causes of the high ratio is the inability of drivers to detect and recognize roadway obstacles and vulnerable road users far away enough to adapt their trajectories. • There was no evidence that reduced street lighting using different adaptive strategies, from an energy savings perspective, is associated with a change in collisions at night. • Among different types of crime, violent crimes against the person have the highest percentage during nighttime. Any effect due to lighting should be most noticeable in the data on violent crime. • Although from a pedestrian’s point of view that more light increases the perception of security, the literature review found that there is no link between lighting and crime, or that any link is too subtle or complex to have been evident in the studies undertaken to date. • Explanations of the positive effects of lighting are that it functions as a situational crime prevention measure that reduces criminal opportunity and perceived rewards and increases perceived risk, and that it serves as a method of strengthening community confidence, cohesion, and social control through more effective street use. • Mixed effects suggest that the results are likely to vary in different conditions, such as the socioeconomic context of the
